one_liner: Tree-hash mode that runs one message as 4 interleaved SHA-256 lanes on AVX; 2-2.5x OpenSSL 1.0.1c, different digests.
what_it_does: j-lanes is a hash construction, not a library. It splits one message into j slices (in the 2012 paper, each 128-bit chunk is dealt out as four 32-bit words, one per slice), hashes each slice with SHA-256, then hashes the concatenation of the j digests in a final 'wrapping' step. The output is a 32-byte digest, but it is not SHA-256(message), so hasher and verifier must both use the mode. The 2014 follow-up (ePrint 2014/170) proposes a one-shot API with the same shape as SHA-256, SHA256_j_lanes(hash, msg, len), notes it can stream in j x 64-byte steps, and adds per-lane IVs and test vectors for j=4, 8 and 16. No code was released.
how_it_is_fast: Serial SHA-256 is one dependent chain of compression calls. Slicing turns one message into j independent messages, which the authors' S-HASH multi-buffer kernel runs with one slice per 32-bit lane of a 128-bit AVX register, so each SIMD Update compresses 4 blocks at once. For a 256x-byte message this costs 4x+7 Updates instead of 4x+1: one padding block per lane plus 3 serial Updates to wrap the 128 bytes of digests. The 4x bulk Updates run 4-wide. Word interleaving means plain sequential loads put each word in the right lane with no transpose. Without SIMD the mode loses: calling OpenSSL once per slice took 13.57 c/B against 12.87 c/B for plain OpenSSL at 8KB.
when_to_use: You own both ends of the format and can define a new digest, for example signed boot or firmware images or an internal integrity manifest, and messages are at least a few KB. The paper measured 1.97x at 2KB rising to 2.53x at 128KB against OpenSSL 1.0.1c.
One long message at a time, where multi-buffer hashing (S-HASH) has nothing to run in parallel.
x86 cores with 128-bit or 256-bit SIMD but no SHA extensions (the paper used Ivy Bridge AVX; the 2014 follow-up also measured Haswell AVX2 with j=8).
As a design reference when specifying a SIMD-friendly tree mode: the 2014 spec gives slicing rules, IV derivation and test vectors.
when_not_to_use: Anywhere a standard SHA-256 value is expected: TLS, HMAC interop, signature schemes, Git or any content address shared with third parties. The digest is different by construction.

Short messages. The fixed wrap and per-lane padding cost is only amortized on longer inputs; the paper says gains are fully realized only for 'sufficiently long' messages, and Intel's similar Multi-Hash paper says benefits diminish below about 1KB.

When you need code today. Nothing was released. The nearest shipping code, Intel ISA-L crypto's mh_sha256 (16 word-interleaved segments), pads and wraps differently, so its digests are not j-lanes digests.

CPUs with SHA extensions. The paper predates them and never compares against them. minio/sha256-simd's README reports 1979 MB/s for SHA-extension SHA-256 on a 3.7 GHz Ryzen 7 2700X, about 1.9 c/B, well under the paper's best 4-lanes figure of 5.05 c/B. The CPUs differ, so treat that comparison as rough.
Settings that need a standardized or formally analysed mode. Security is argued only by pointing to general tree-hashing theory, and the author's own recommended j moved from 8 (2012) to 16 (2014).

integration.form: not applicable: a paper and specification only, with no code released
integration.dependencies: not documented (no code). The measured implementation was built on the authors' unreleased S-HASH AVX kernel.
integration.min_toolchain: not documented: the paper gives no compiler, version or flags
integration.platforms: The construction is portable. Measurements are on x86-64 with AVX (Core i7-3770, Ivy Bridge), and the 2014 follow-up also used Haswell (AVX2). Scalar or per-slice serial evaluation works but is slower than plain SHA-256.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. The paper notes the slices can also be spread across cores.

gotchas: There are two incompatible versions. The 2012 mode uses the standard SHA-256 IV everywhere, while the 2014 spec prepends per-lane prefix blocks (lane index, j, a mode byte and 'SHA256'), which gives different IVs and different digests. Pin the spec version and j, because the digest depends on both.

The 2014 spec text slices by 32-bit words, but its j=4 test-vector lanes are interleaved in 64-byte blocks (lane 0 is message bytes 0-63, 256-319, 512-575 and 768-831). Resolve this against the vectors before implementing.

With j=4, a length not divisible by 256 bytes leaves at least one slice a different length and needs special last-Update handling (the paper calls the cost negligible). Very short messages give empty slices, which are hashed as the empty message. Choosing j above the SIMD width adds wrap Updates: at 8KB, 16-lanes needs 153 Updates against 135 for 4-lanes.
The SHA-3 comparison in Fig. 4 is close. At 8KB, 4-lanes SHA-256 took 5.46 c/B against 5.74 for 4-lanes BLAKE-512 and 5.82 for plain BLAKE-512, a margin of about 5-7%.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick j-lanes over S-HASH only when there is a single long message in flight and you control the digest format. S-HASH needs many independent messages but keeps standard SHA-256 outputs. Against minio/sha256-simd, which is shipping Go code that produces standard digests (with SHA-extension, ARM64 and AVX-512 multi-buffer paths), j-lanes is only a design option for a new format on hardware without SHA instructions.
verified_claims_summary: On a Core i7-3770 (Ivy Bridge; Hyper-Threading, Turbo and SpeedStep off; RDTSC, minimum of 5 runs of 100,000 iterations), AVX 4-lanes SHA-256 took 6.75 c/B at 2KB and 5.05 c/B at 128KB, against 13.27 and 12.78 c/B for OpenSSL 1.0.1c's serial SHA-256 (1.97-2.53x) and 10.45-10.09 c/B for the authors' improved n-SMS serial code (1.55-2x). No compiler or flags are given, and the outputs are j-lanes digests, not SHA-256 digests.
status_note: This is finished research: ePrint 2012/476, republished in Journal of Information Security 4(1):7-11 (2013, a SCIRP journal, 2 Crossref citations), plus a 2014 follow-up spec with test vectors (ePrint 2014/170, CC BY). No code or standard adoption turned up in the sources read, and the closest shipping relative, ISA-L's mh_sha256, is not digest-compatible.
